title: Intriguing connections in Anja Bihlmaier & BBC Philharmonic's Prom including Mahler's Das Lied von der Erde with Jamie Barton & Clay Hilley, yet perhaps better heard on BBC Sounds
author: Planet Hugill
content:
| ![Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Anja Bihilmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Anja Bihilmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou)](<https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgpE8cuPNGWzJj_H7FaOaiS6zm7WzYqZPhPfHd2Bm2Fmrzg9eqh7gHWqD3jcgGQ2hNbyrIwGEa7y1mOrAoc8CjViwaVG78roIph-okWGwBlV-eb30zfj_Jpgs-gKMf9cRD-uZpUQNFkbohHrhjatEeqxbd9t-8opL1pnTzXBeHiGjEMGhBB1BlTUQ/w426-h640/BBC%20Proms_Mahler%E2%80%99s%20%E2%80%98Song%20of%20the%20Earth%E2%80%99_photocredit%20BBC%20Chris%20Christodoulou_21.08.26%20(7).jpg>) | 
| Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) | 
Bushra El-Turk: Mosaic, Haydn: Symphony No. 45 in F sharp minor, 'Farewell', Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde; Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, BBC Philharmonic Orchestra, Anja Bihlmaier
Reviewed 21 August 2026
A rare performance of one of Haydn's best-known early symphonies alongside Mahler's glorious final symphonic utterance in a concert full of links and references in performances that did not always quite overcome the challenges of the Royal Albert Hall
The BBC Prom at the Royal Albert Hall on Friday 21 August might, at first, have seemed a typical Proms programme presenting a diverse trio of works. The BBC Philharmonic Orchestra and their principal guest conductor, Anja Bihlmaier presented us with Bushra El-Turk's Mosaic, Haydn's Farewell Symphony, and Mahler's Das Lied von der Erde with Jamie Barton and Clay Hilley.
Diverse works, to be sure, but scratch under the surface and we saw the connective tissues. The subject of a farewell linked Haydn and Mahler in a way that was sufficiently contrasting as to be intriguing. And then Bushra El-Turk's work addresses issues of cross-pollination between cultures, finding elements of the rootlessness and otherness that Mahler found in the Chinese poetry he set in Das Lied von der Erde. It was a lavish programme too, the huge orchestra for the Mahler not used in the first half. I did wonder whether Bihlmaier should have had the courage of her convictions and performed Haydn with Mahleresque forces (large body of strings, four oboes, five horns). Go on, it sounds intriguing and after all what are festival for?
Bushra El-Turk's Mosaic was written for the Manchester Camerata for the 2009/10 season. It began with a scurrying shimmer on the strings that was so quiet as to be almost inaudible in the Royal Albert Hall. Dramatic fragments and motifs emerged over, creating an anxious, almost unnerving feel. A gradual build-up led to denser textures but the fragments never quite coalesced, until at the end in ravishing quiet we heard a romantic, rather hymn-like figure emerge. I would have liked to hear the piece in more sympathetic circumstances to bring out the detail.
Because of the circumstances of its first performance, and the rather intriguing meta-theatre woven in to the music in a very contemporary manner, Haydn's Farewell Symphony is amongst the best known of his earlier ones. Yet it has not been performed at the Proms since 1938, and this was only its fourth performance! It was brave of Bihlmaier to decide to do it with a modern instrument orchestra and all credit to her. We should her more Haydn like this.
| ![Haydn: Farewell Symphony - Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) Haydn: Farewell Symphony - Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou)](<https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiy-cuBhHWhlcYIEq0SHSWU_3MW-87dhtc7z8Ep161Ai8NS-45XqCmN4qBrcyJ4kdB5gwCnty3xs5hukMr1ydFI2AYRwBG-GufasQB409jjMC-DiD36bd6QSeSF0_tzTAaJD7ISQfQ2NbeVppMxY7Dyh_zLQRSrjDZ9wWzNXT6xZ1RqqeWYbKCG6A/w640-h426/BBC%20Proms_Mahler%E2%80%99s%20%E2%80%98Song%20of%20the%20Earth%E2%80%99_photocredit%20BBC%20Chris%20Christodoulou_21.08.26%20(10).jpg>) | 
| Haydn: Farewell Symphony - Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) | 
In the first movement, the strings were strong, stylish yet completely modern. With a large-ish string body, the wind rather receded in the balance, yet there was urgency and dynamism to the performance with a lovely lyricism in the central episode. The slow movement was quiet with intimate detail, pointed motifs and lyrical moments. Yet there was harmonic uncertainty too, for all the standard feel of the movement the music was not obvious. I was worried about Bilhmaier's choice of tempo: not that slow, but with the repeats it made the movement too long for its surroundings, yet her tempos gave space for the detail. The Menuetto was full of contrasts, delicacy against strength, alongside the pull of the key relationships. All ending in wonderful midair. The finale was crisp and urgent, again full of contrasts with energetic impulse against elegant slow lyricism. As the instrumental body reduced (and the players did leave the stage) we went on a sort of time-lapse performance towards the modern day impulse for small scale performance. And the ending was as weird and mysterious as it should be.
Mahler's orchestra for Das Lied von der Erde is huge, with quadruple woodwind and much else besides including the mandolins. Throughout the performance the BBC Philharmonic was indeed resplendent. Bihlmaier took a disciplined almost classical approach, yet relishing all the tonal and timbral contrasts that Mahler implies. Speeds were steady-ish yet fluid with space for the singers. And yet... I suspect this is one of those performances that will sound better when rebalance for the radio. Somehow, neither singer quite dominated or cut through the orchestra when push came to shove. There were plenty of good moments, but you had to concentrate hard.
| ![Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou)](<https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiJUVK42I6euxXFnakG5FXpbtDiwgTn7xxZKOvzNumOMC0rtaIkxLGKvNwIdWkV0cMa2_Zm0lSCklhorXqRFa0iR0a8axQ6QzI-3uQuuVVgR3N3Mz_zTaO45zyNNH7n6qopA_OxsXfQXpLAgohUIqI2jidHjgCIwojbwflPx5CE_2XsrUK_crayWA/w640-h426/BBC%20Proms_Mahler%E2%80%99s%20%E2%80%98Song%20of%20the%20Earth%E2%80%99_photocredit%20BBC%20Chris%20Christodoulou_21.08.26%20(4).jpg>) | 
| Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) | 
For 'Drinking song of the earth's misery', Clay Hilley's approach leaned on a vivid dramatic presentation, and a clear histrionic effort to communicate the dramatic narrative of the song. By the end of the song, his anger was surprisingly fierce. Yet his unforced, focused tone meant that his voice was somewhat recessed in the balance. Hilley took so much care with the dramatic detail and narrative that I wished we could have been in closer contact. For 'The lonely on in Autumn', Bihlmaier began with barely there strings and a fabulous oboe solo. Jamie Barton was a dignified presence, and she seemed to choose emotion over simple beauty of tone. Towards the end there were moments of letting go, but mostly this was a contained yet intense account of the song. One which did not always cut through the orchestra.
Hilley brought a delightful lightness of touch to 'Youth' with very pointed words and the sense that he was telling a story. The orchestra was light and delicate for the opening of 'Beauty' contrasting with Barton's rather darker, steadier approach. She was telling a story and somewhat relished the contrast between voice and orchestra. I loved the way Bihlmaier got the orchestra to dip and dance, but her and later in the work I was rather wishing for some portamentos to enliven the clean string lines. In the faster, vivid sections, Barton's detail was rather lost in the hall though I loved the sense of impulse. In the moments when the orchestra relaxed and gave her space, her delight was palpable.
'The drunkard in Spring' featured Hilley back in storytelling mode, and oh boy was he vividly histrionic, yet some terrific detail was lost though the climaxes of the verses were terrific. We ended with bravura histrionics and came to appreciate his lively engaged storytelling. Then came 'Farewell' (Der Abschied). For the opening, Bihlmaier brought out the lower instruments and that tam tam to create some aural magic. There was space here for Barton, and she was artful yet affecting, but dignified too. I almost felt she was feeling the weight of the pressure of performing this work in this hall (following on from Janet Baker's four performance and Jessye Norman's one with Rattle and Jon Vickers!). Barton's dignified emoting was paired with some strong orchestral colours and a constant sense of impetus allied to fluid tempos. Towards the end of the first half we did get more expansive phrases, yet there was also the magic of her quiet intensity contrasting with just the solo flute. But at the end of the first part it was touch and go who won the loudness battle! In the second part, Barton was dignified, the music flowing yet with classical discipline. In the final stanza she did let do, though the repeated 'Ewig' was very internal and concentrated.
| ![Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou)](<https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhTZRZ-7Sh05ia_8ghebTfAU7xIz-Obsqqy_M3yQqoMyUCuN-ZRKJopDgmUO5RPr_iQgTlyE7RG86CutNEAMWHJxYhZLUChHCa6LCoRAHzvrhKCAy7lYVTqnO4-b7Sijc-aeuOIvrQwmuRYh32B7zui-cLfX7AGgq2te3kI3VahzFWMTInqMDCxqA/w640-h426/BBC%20Proms_Mahler%E2%80%99s%20%E2%80%98Song%20of%20the%20Earth%E2%80%99_photocredit%20BBC%20Chris%20Christodoulou_21.08.26%20(3).jpg>) | 
| Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) | 
The concert is on BBC Sounds.
The blog is free, but I'd be delighted if you were to show your appreciation by buying me a coffee.

title: Video: GLENGARRY GLEN ROSS Star Indira Varma Talks 'Plays…
author: Rachel Stone
content:
The Old Vic shared a new installment of its 'Plays That Made Me' series featuring Indira Varma, who stopped by the Script Library in the theatre's Backstage Cafe & Bar before heading to the main stage to appear as Levene in GLENGARRY GLEN ROSS. The video, titled "Indira Varma on why it's so wonderful to be 'horrible'", finds Varma pulling five scripts from the shelves and discussing what drew her to each one.
Varma's selections span a wide range of genres and eras, moving through Celebration, The Dance of Death, Macbeth, The Seagull and Faith Healer. According to the video description, the common thread across her picks is fascinating characters written by brilliant writers, a theme that connects directly to her current role as Levene in David Mamet's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama.
GLENGARRY GLEN ROSS is currently running at The Old Vic in an all-female production directed by Tony Award winner Patrick Marber, with Rosa Salazar starring opposite Varma as Roma. The production reimagines Mamet's story of cutthroat real estate salesmen with a cast that also includes Mercedes Bahleda, Nancy Crane, Dorothea Myer-Bennett, Florence Odumosu and Niky Wardle.
The Script Library visit offers a glimpse into Varma's own reading habits and the works she considers formative, tying her personal taste in drama to the characters she brings to life on stage.
summary: Indira Varma featured in a new installment of The Old Vic's 'Plays That Made Me' video series, discussing five formative scripts at the Backstage Cafe & Bar's Script Library. Varma's selections include Celebration, The Dance of Death, Macbeth, The Seagull, and Faith Healer, united by their fascinating characters and brilliant writers. She is currently starring as Levene in an all-female production of David Mamet's Glengarry Glen Ross at The Old Vic.
key_points: Indira Varma appeared in the latest video for The Old Vic's 'Plays That Made Me' series.
She selected and discussed five scripts: Celebration, The Dance of Death, Macbeth, The Seagull, and Faith Healer.
Her picks are tied together by their brilliant writers and fascinating characters.
Varma currently stars as Levene in an all-female production of Glengarry Glen Ross at The Old Vic, directed by Patrick Marber.

title: Review. Bottomless Sundays at Bocconcino. -
author: Nick Harman
content:
Sunday in Soho? What could be nicer, and a nice change from Sunday Roast. Nick finds his stomach isn’t bottomless, but he had a good time stressing it out.
![](https://www.foodepedia.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_6943.jpeg)
When I was a kid, a birthday treat was visiting Hamley’s in Regent Street to pick out one, reasonably priced toy. I loved it, but what I liked even more was having something to eat later in Spaghetti House. It’s hard for people born later to appreciate what it was like to have exotic food as a kid.
Sadly now Spaghetti House has gone, we walked past its shuttered remains on the way to Bocconcino, but in Bocconcino something of Spag House’s warm spirit has been reborn.
Pizza and pasta in a nice friendly environment, with fast service and reasonable prices
And now, a Sunday feast that’s available every Sunday from 1pm to 3.30pm, a bottomless brunch that we found defeated us, in the nicest possible way. All the pasta and pizza you can eat is a bit of a two edged sword because most humans can’t eat that much.
Still, it was well worth trying.
![](https://www.foodepedia.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_6956.jpeg)
It’s a really nice room; large without feeling cavernous and very attractively decked out. The sort of place that’s ideal for groups and indeed there was one there when we arrived and already in the party spirit. So I asked to be seated a little way away, I am not a killjoy but I could see they were going to get noisier. Especially when the DJ came on. Which is again, fine.
Anyhoo. The Brunch. The deal is a big plate of Italian antipasti first, with mozzarella, arancini, tomato and stracciatella bruschetta, pickled vegetables, mixed olives, a selection of Italian salumi and carasau bread.
This was generous and we piled in eagerly, having of course skipped breakfast in preperation. Nothing was unlikeable, not even the pickled cauliflower,  and we happily went through it at pace.
The ‘bottomless’ also applies to Prosecco, but we ‘kicked it up a notch’ as Jamie would say by paying a few quid more for unlimited Aperol and Luxardo Limoncello Spritz. I do like Aperol, that bitterness makes me happy.
With plates cleared, we chose our pasta. I do enjoy a Carbonara made properly with pigs’ cheeks, (guanciale), eggs, Pecorino Romano and black pepper. I make it at home a lot, albeit with boring old pancetta. I seem to have mastered the art of not scrambling the eggs.
![](https://www.foodepedia.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Snapseed-4.jpeg)
![](https://www.foodepedia.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Snapseed-2-1.jpeg)
Obviously Bocconcino has too, although I thought there was perhaps a bit too much egg as it pooled at the bottom of the fabulously coloured plates that we both really wanted to steal (we didn’t). The guanciale was semi crispy and saline, the pasta tubes just right, cooked just under al dente so they could soften as they absorbed  the sauce at the last minute.
The restaurant’s signature Black Truffle Tagliatelle is actually extra money, so P went for its close cousin, Pappardelle with wild mushrooms and stracciatella. Stracciatella is a stringy cheese that forms the heart of Burrata and it’s rather delicious. P loved this dish.
Although pasta portions were sensible, we were now feeling rather full. Our nice waiter encouraged us to have another pasta dish, it was after all a bottomless brunch, but we resisted and moved on to pizza.
![](https://www.foodepedia.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_6966.jpeg)
I clocked the pizza oven going in, it looked proper and not one of those metal jobs. Gas fired,  I suspect, which is okay, and with a rotating base which seems a good upgrade to ensure the pizzas are evenly cooked.
Ours came out the way I like them. There is no ‘perfect pizza’, as they vary across Italy but I like a blistered crust and a thin base almost liquid in the centre. A pizza to eat with a knife and fork. This was it.
My Diavola had all it needed; a rich tomato sauce, the right amount of mozzarella and generous amounts of spicy salami.  I actually like my Diavolas a teeny bit hotter, but this was hot enough.
P had a Quattro Stagioni Tomato Sauce, Mozzarella, Ham, Mushrooms, Olives, Artichokes, you can’t go wrong with a Quattro. Again very nice, very large, very filling.
The DJ was on by now and the room was filling up, a good atmosphere. The nice waiter encouraged us to have another pizza each, and much as we wanted to in theory, in practice we were stuffed. So we had some more drinks instead.
My verdict ? Bocconcino is a good place for decent Italian food served in a modern relaxed style. The Sunday Brunch is a very good deal IF you eat and drink a lot, otherwise it’s still a good deal but you’re not saving all that much.
So go hungry and frighten the nice waiters!
Bottomless Prosecco is included in the £49 per person package, while guests can also opt for unlimited Aperol or Luxardo Limoncello Spritz for £56 per person.
Following Sunday brunch, guests can settle in for £7 cocktails, classic Italian spritzes and crafted drinks, paired with a selection of cicchetti from the kitchen.
Bocconcino Soho
59 Great Marlborough St, London W1F 7JY
@bocconcinolondon
summary: Bocconcino in Soho offers a bottomless Sunday brunch featuring all-you-can-eat antipasti, pasta, and pizza, accompanied by a live DJ and drinks. Reviewer Nick and his dining companion found the generous portions filling and delicious, praising the quality of the dishes and the lively atmosphere. The brunch package costs £49 per person with bottomless Prosecco, or £56 per person for an upgraded option including unlimited Aperol or Luxardo Limoncello Spritz.
key_points: The Sunday brunch runs every Sunday from 1pm to 3.30pm at Bocconcino Soho.
The meal starts with a generous Italian antipasti plate followed by unlimited choices of pasta and pizza.
Bottomless Prosecco is included in the £49 package, while unlimited Aperol or Luxardo Limoncello Spritz is available for £56.
The restaurant features a lively atmosphere with a DJ, fast service, and an attractive dining room suitable for groups.

title: Brian Hyland performs outside Downing Street for NHS campaign
author: PA News Agency
content:
Brian Hyland has performed outside Downing Street to raise awareness for an NHS campaign.
The American musician, 82, joined British singer and campaigner Ashleigh Harley on Saturday, where they performed his hit Itsy Bity Teeny Weeny Yellow Polka Dot Bikini.
The pair played guitars and sung into a microphone set up outside the Prime Minister’s Office, where they were joined by others backing the campaign.
It aims to raise awareness of the number of young people who struggle to be diagnosed by the NHS and improve outcomes for patients facing delayed diagnosis of complex conditions.
![Brian Hyland and Ashleigh Harley playing guitars and singing outside Downing Street.](https://image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/eb40c8d8380ee194433dd610c48013d8Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3NDk0ODQw/2.85628126.jpg?w=640)
Harley was 12 when she had her first seizure and started to become ill, but it took more than a decade before she was diagnosed, after her mother did her own research.
She previously told the Press Association: “I got seizures every day, which made school completely impossible because I was collapsing every day.
“I couldn’t see. I was getting paralysis quite badly, so I couldn’t use my hands. I couldn’t write down stuff. That was the first episode, that was when we realised something was wrong.
“We went down every single different route, and the doctors couldn’t figure out what it was. And there was the stipulation of, young people don’t get ill, therefore, you know, just go away and get on with it. It’ll be all right.”
![Brian Hyland and Ashleigh Harley playing guitars and singing outside Downing Street.](https://image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/bfeb97491318f760b474f0dbf6264698Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3NDk0OTg5/2.85628135.jpg?w=640)
However, Harley never recovered, and lost the ability to eat and speak and had to use a computer to communicate. She was eventually sent home from hospital to die.
She continued: “It actually was my mum who had to do all the research to figure out exactly what it was, figure out the sort of specialists we needed to talk to, and then as soon as she figured that out, then I was able to get treatment.”
Harley was eventually diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), a genetic condition that weakens connective tissue, which progressed into severe gastroparesis and refeeding syndrome, a life-threatening condition with a 15% survival rate.
![Ashleigh Harley raising her arms up smiling while a guitar rests in on her chest](https://image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/b32290f5f561fb4a28baa51fbe74c310Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3NDk0OTAw/2.85628127.jpg?w=640)
She went on to say waiting for a diagnosis “ruined” her youth, which she had since discovered had been the experience of many other young people.
Harley has now founded a charity, Save Our Lives, to improve diagnostic protocols, and has released a cover of Itsy Bitsy Teenie Weenie Yellow Polkadot Bikini to raise funds.
The charity hopes to launch a new service adjacent to the NHS to speed up the diagnosis process and improve treatments for those suffering from delayed diagnosis.
Hyland previously told PA: “It touches me immensely because it’s such a tragic situation with children having their childhood taken away.”
summary: American musician Brian Hyland performed outside Downing Street alongside British singer Ashleigh Harley to raise awareness for an NHS campaign. The initiative aims to highlight the struggles young people face with delayed medical diagnoses and to improve patient outcomes for complex conditions. The campaign aims to raise awareness about young people struggling with delayed diagnoses for complex medical conditions.
Ashleigh Harley experienced a decade-long delay in diagnosis before discovering she had Ehlers-Danlos syndrome through her mother's research.

title: Campaigners demand action as disabled high-rise tenants left at risk of Grenfell-style tragedy
author: Enfield Dispatch
content:
Despite new regulations many disabled tenants continue to feel unsafe reports Kumail Jaffer, Local Democracy Reporter
![A woman sitting on a chair talking to a man in a wheelchair](https://enfielddispatch.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/WhatsApp_Image_2026-08-12_at_15.36.52-1024x768.jpeg)
Disabled Londoners in high rise flats are still living in fear over their safety if a fire was to break out, a leading campaigner has said.
Fifteen of the 37 disabled residents living in Grenfell Tower at the time of the 2017 blaze lost their lives – equivalent to 41 per cent. Five years later, the inquiry into the tragedy recommended that personalised evacuation plans be issued to residents of tower blocks with disabilities or reduced mobility.
These eventually came into force in April, meaning disabled Londoners in specific residential buildings have been able to request tailored emergency escape support from their landlords or housing providers.
However, campaigners have raised concerns over the regulations, which mean disabled residents will only be eligible for a Residential Personal Emergency Evacuation Plan (RPEEP) if they live in buildings which are over 18 metres or seven storeys, or buildings between 11 and 18 metres tall with a ‘simultaneous’ evacuation strategy.
Those in buildings under 11 metres tall are not entitled to a plan under the rules.
Adam Gabsi, Co-Chair of Inclusion London, told the London Assembly Fire Committee in June that many disabled social housing residents, including him, continue to feel unsafe in their homes.
“Smoke does not discriminate based on height,” he said. “If smoke was to rise to the seventh floor, it is not going to stop, and likewise, a fire does not discriminate based on where you are. If someone is disabled on the ground floor, the first floor, the second floor, they are still disabled.
“What are we waiting for, my building, me to burn? What are we waiting for here?”
On a visit to Gabsi’s flat in Harrow, North West London, the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) identified several major concerns, including damp, mould, and – crucial in any evacuation – broken lifts.
Gabsi, who lives on the sixth floor of Trident Point, said he has little confidence that he would make it out alive if there was a fire in the block, which is run by Metropolitan Thames Valley Housing (MTVH).
“If the fire alarm was to ring here, I would have a serious issue with getting outside,” he said. “Previously, I found the evacuation chair to be locked behind a cupboard of which I don’t have the code, which kind of negates the purpose for it.
“I’ve also been told that it can only be used by firefighters, which again doesn’t amount to equal evacuation processes.
“There is a fire safe lift – however, that lift is not working. So what is the point? There is total negligence by by the housing provider and housing association.
“There aren’t arrangements [for a fire]. At this point, I’m going to say a prayer and just stay in my house, to be honest.”
Last month the Fire Committee wrote to the mayor to demand more engagement between social housing landlords and residents.
Chair Anne Clarke, a Labour Assembly member, said: “Nine years after the Grenfell Tower fire, we heard compelling evidence that many social housing residents continue to feel unsafe in their homes. No Londoner should live in fear of fire safety.”
Deputy chair Hina Bokhari, who has long held City Hall to account over the plight of disabled Londoners, said the current situation was “outrageous”.
“What Adam and the residents in this building having to deal with – I’m close to tears,” the Liberal Democrat assembly member told the LDRS.
“If there is a fire here, if something terrible happened here, do we see another Grenfell? Yes – that is my blunt and honest opinion.
“Everybody who lives in high rise flats are at risk. And when it comes to disabled residents, I’m actually really depressed. I feel as if they’re signing a death wish by living here in a high rise flat now.
“Things haven’t moved on since Grenfell – it is absolutely outrageous that we’re in this situation. We still haven’t got accessible housing that is affordable for disabled Londoners. The mayor is not doing his job.”
Gabsi added: “He is pandering to developers rather than really thinking about Londoners – the safety of disabled people should be paramount.
“We not a fringe group, we’re not a small group, and we are the one marginalised group that anyone could join at any time. The fact that this is not being taken seriously is very disappointing.”
What is the mayor doing about it?
City Hall plans to publish a Disability Action Plan next month. The document will make a series of commitments on housing, employment, transport, community safety and accessing services.
A spokesperson for the mayor said: “For many years the mayor strongly lobbied the previous Government to introduce legislation for RPEEPs and welcomed the introduction of this law in April this year.
“He has continued to encourage the government to widen the scope of the new legislation to incorporate all residential blocks and for there to be central funding to pay for them, as well as pushing building owners and landlords to implement these plans as soon as possible.
“It is vital that ministers continue to work with deaf and disabled groups to ensure the legislation and guidance is as effective as it can be, and to monitor how these plans are being implemented across the country. The mayor is also committed to working with the London Fire Brigade and local authorities to ensure disabled Londoners have safe evacuation routes and appropriate support during emergencies.”
An MTVH housing association spokesperson said: “We understand the concerns raised by residents with regards to the issues they have experienced at Trident Point. Their safety and wellbeing is our top priority and we are working closely with them to identify appropriate support to ensure effective arrangements are in place in the event of an emergency evacuation.
“At Trident Point, Personal Emergency Evacuation Plans are in place for residents with identified evacuation needs. We are currently reviewing and updating these plans with residents to ensure they reflect new legal requirements.
“We recognise that there have been intermittent reliability issues with the lifts installed at Trident Point in 2022 and 2023. We continue to work with the lift contractor, landlords and the building’s managing agents, Y&Y and Orbit, to deliver a long-term solution. Whenever a lift outage occurs, we proactively contact affected residents to review support arrangements and determine whether any additional measures are required.
“Leaks, which resulted in water damage, have been resolved. We are now working with Y&Y to complete remedial works and address any remaining damage.”

Specific issues highlighted at Trident Point include broken fire-safe lifts and inaccessible evacuation chairs, leaving disabled tenants feeling unsafe. While housing association MTVH states they are reviewing evacuation plans and addressing lift issues, London Assembly members and activists demand broader legislation and stronger action from the mayor.

Metropolitan Thames Valley Housing stated they are reviewing evacuation plans and working on long-term solutions for the building's intermittent lift issues.

title: Ban L plate moped riders from deliveries on London roads, ministers told
author: Kumail Jaffer
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Delivery drivers targeted in immigration enforcement crackdown](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/12/05/9/58/HomeOfficeDeliveryDrivers.JPG?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
The qualification, which usually takes a single day to obtain, is valid for two years and can be renewed repeatedly without any requirement to progress to a full driving test.
The London Assembly last month passed a motion calling on the Government to prohibit the use of provisional licences for commercial work, including food delivery driving, to improve safety for all road users.
“The CBT was built as a way for people to learn the roads and build up that knowledge,” he told the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS).
“Because you can’t learn on a bike the same way you’re learning a car, because with a car [you are] with an instructor who will have his own set of pedals.
“It wasn’t built for indefinite use. You’ve got people who are now working into delivery drivers, commercially working on the roads. This is not a qualification to drive on the road. We’ve got to end that practice.
“It is clear these are a menace to the road – if I’m in Bromley Town Centre, and I’m going home, I will see multiple offences on the way home, L plate motorbikes mounting the pavement, for example.
“This is dangerous behaviour from people who think they are ready to drive on the road because they’ve done their CBT.
Read More
“But they just aren’t, and that’s the real problem in this, that they’re not ready to drive on the road because this is their basic qualification, and there is no incentive to get that full licence.”
![The Home Office led an operation targeting delivery drivers across London and the UK](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/12/05/9/58/HomeOfficeDeliveryDrivers.JPG?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
In 2022, the Mayor of London told Assembly Members that he “firmly believes” that the current CBT is “not fit for purpose and is not an appropriate level of qualification, particularly for those driving for work”.
He claimed TfL has no powers to regulate private companies, meaning the authority could not mandate couriers to ride on a full licence. These powers lie at a national level.
Earlier this year ministers launched a consultation on changes to moped and motorcycle training, which could involve CBT certificate reform.
Rebecca Paul, the MP for Reigate, attempted to table an amendment to the Crime and Policing Act, which was passed in April, to ban learner moped drivers from undertaking commercial activity using the roads. However, it was unsuccessful.
Louie French, the MP for Old Bexley and Sidcup, told the LDRS: “The Labour Government has lost control of delivery drivers abusing the L plate system.
“High streets and roads across the country are now littered with men using mopeds to deliver food.
“The Government must urgently grip this situation to ensure that all delivery drivers are working here legally and are not endangering other road users.”
Mr Turrell said the biggest barrier to reform may be “pushback” from major employers such as Just Eat, Deliveroo and Uber.
“It’ll be interesting to see whether the Government do have the stomach to take this on,” he added.
“They’ve been consulting on it, so I couldn’t say whether or not they’re dragging their feet or reluctant for sure, but I think it will be telling over the coming months to find out whether this is something that they want to get their teeth stuck into.”
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “As part of our road safety strategy, the DVSA consulted on reforms to moped and motorcycle training and testing, including whether there should be a time limit on CBT certification. We are now analysing the responses, with the aim of improving safety and modernising motorcycling.”
A Just Eat spokesperson said: “The safety of all road users is extremely important to Just Eat.
“Last year we were the first food delivery platform to partner with the leading road safety charity Brake, and we provide regular guidance on safety and responsible behaviour.
“We actively support stronger regulation and robust enforcement to tackle modified e-bikes and requiring moped riders to have a full licence. We remain committed to working with authorities and our industry peers to ensure the roads are safe for all users.”
Deliveroo and Uber Eats were contacted for comment.
summary: Ministers and the London Assembly are facing calls to ban L-plate moped and motorcycle riders from engaging in commercial delivery work on London roads. Critics argue that the Compulsory Basic Training (CBT) certificate, which can be renewed indefinitely without a full driving test, is being abused and leads to dangerous road behavior. While the Government launched a consultation on motorcycle training reforms, delivery platforms like Just Eat have expressed support for requiring moped riders to hold a full license.
key_points: The London Assembly passed a motion urging the Government to ban provisional license holders from commercial delivery work.
The Compulsory Basic Training (CBT) certificate can be repeatedly renewed without requiring a full driving test.
Critics and MPs warn that L-plate delivery riders pose safety risks, citing instances of dangerous riding behavior like mounting pavements.
The Department for Transport is analyzing responses from a recent consultation on moped and motorcycle training reforms.
Delivery platform Just Eat stated its support for requiring moped riders to have a full license.

title: Travellers 'intimidated' by campaign against new caravan site in north London
author: Josef Steen
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/22/12/11/LGT-at-town-hall-edit-2.jpg?trim=389,0,188,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) The community currently has no permanent pitches in the borough, For many Gypsies and Travellers, living in a caravan is a core part of their ethnicity and cultural heritage. Under the Housing Act 2004, Islington’s Labour-run council has to identify and meet the accommodation needs of Gypsies and Travellers, but has long struggled to do so – until 2025, when nine possible sites were put forward. ![

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/22/12/11/LGT-at-town-hall-edit-2.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) The latest proposals include turning a small green space on a council estate, Aubert Court, into a pitch for members of the community already living in social housing there or nearby. A petition from ‘Friends of Aubert Park’, which has now reached 1,800 signatures, argues that the plans are unsuitable given the dearth of green spaces in Islington. “We support the need to provide suitable accommodation for Gypsy and Traveller families, but this should not come at the cost of one of Islington’s scarce parks,” the petition states. “Once this space is gone, it is gone.” One member of the Traveller community, Lisa Casey, 58, told the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) that caretakers on Aubert Court were warning residents they would be “overrun with Travellers and feral children”. “It’s not even a park,” she said. “The land on Aubert Park is disused, you can only use it if you’re a resident. We’re taking a small portion of it. Why can’t we live within the community? “We already exist. We’ve been here probably a lot longer than a lot of these residents. We just want to give up our council homes we already live in and go back to our cultural roots.” ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/22/13/02/The_proposed_sites_at_Aubert_Court.JPG?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Ms Casey, who was born in the borough, added that she had in the past been the target of abuse and had her car vandalised after appearing at a meeting about a different pitch site at Ronalds Road. Read More Mena Mongan, from advocacy group London Gypsies and Travellers, said her organisation had been contacted by local residents who judged the objections were being driven by “pure discrimination”. “I’m downhearted about all this. I’ve seen it far too often,” Ms Mongan told the LDRS, claiming that opponents to the scheme are presenting deep opposition by “getting comments from every Tom, Dick and Harry” without considering the consequences. “These people have nothing better to do with their money than playing with people’s lives,” she added. Ms Mongan referred to academic data showing suicide rates are six to seven times higher among Gypsies and Travellers than the general population. “The council has got to get on top of this,” she added. According to YouGov, nearly half (45 per cent) of the general population would be “uncomfortable” with a Gypsy or Traveller moving next door to them. The LDRS previously reported council officers last year were forced to cut some “discriminatory” remarks from an earlier consultation report on the nine possible sites. “This is extremely challenging in a high-density borough like Islington which has very limited land for development.” The council is now reviewing responses to the consultation, which closed on Tuesday, August 18. However, it is still accepting late representations via email, post or online surveys until September 1. The spokesperson added that the plans would later be reviewed by an independent Planning Inspector. The LDRS contacted Friends of Aubert Park for further comment, but at the time of publication the group had not responded.
summary: Islington Council is reviewing proposals to create a caravan pitch for Gypsy and Traveller families at Aubert Court to meet legal accommodation duties. The plans have sparked a petition with 1,800 signatures over the loss of green space, while members of the Traveller community and advocates report facing intimidation and discrimination during the consultation process. The council is continuing to accept late representations on the proposals until September 1 before they are reviewed by an independent Planning Inspector.
key_points: Under the Housing Act 2004, Islington Council is legally required to identify and meet the accommodation needs of Gypsies and Travellers.
A proposal to turn a green space at Aubert Court into a caravan pitch has drawn a petition with 1,800 signatures citing a lack of local parks.
Members of the Traveller community and advocacy groups reported facing intimidation, discrimination, and vandalism during the consultation.
The consultation closed on August 18, but late representations are being accepted until September 1 before the plans go to an independent Planning Inspector.

title: Video: Ralph Rugoff Tours ANISH KAPOOR Exhibition at Hayward Gallery
author: Rachel Stone
content:
Southbank Centre has shared a video titled 'The Art of Bending Reality,' featuring Hayward Gallery Director Ralph Rugoff giving a personal tour through THE ART OF BENDING REALITY, the gallery's current exhibition of work by artist Anish Kapoor. In the video, Rugoff describes Kapoor as an artist who 'is constantly challenging our conventional ways of seeing things,' guiding viewers through several of the show's large-scale sculptures.
The tour opens with All of Nothing (2026), described as the largest sculpture ever presented at Hayward Gallery, with only portions visible at any one time to preserve what Rugoff calls a sense of mystery. Other works featured include Mount Moriah (2022), a piece Rugoff frames as sombre yet playful, and Ha Makom (2026), a new installation coated in red pigment that sets up a tension between landscape and architecture. The tour also covers two series: Ritual Expiation (2025-2026), visceral pieces suggesting the remains of a ritual sacrifice, and Descent into Limbo (1992), which Kapoor has described as 'not an empty hole but a hole filled with darkness.'
The tour concludes outside the gallery at Tsunami (2025), a curved sculpture that reflects its surroundings in unpredictable ways, continuing what Rugoff frames as Kapoor's ongoing interest in complicating the idea that seeing is believing.
THE ART OF BENDING REALITY is on view at Hayward Gallery through October 18, 2026.
summary: Southbank Centre released a video featuring Hayward Gallery Director Ralph Rugoff guiding viewers through Anish Kapoor's exhibition, 'The Art of Bending Reality.' The tour highlights several large-scale sculptures and installations that challenge conventional ways of seeing. The exhibition is on view at the Hayward Gallery through October 18, 2026.
key_points: Hayward Gallery Director Ralph Rugoff leads a video tour of Anish Kapoor's exhibition titled 'The Art of Bending Reality.'
Featured artworks include the massive sculpture All of Nothing, Mount Moriah, Ha Makom, Ritual Expiation, Descent into Limbo, and Tsunami.
The exhibition explores Kapoor's ongoing interest in complicating the idea that seeing is believing.
The exhibition runs at the Hayward Gallery through October 18, 2026.

“Smoke does not discriminate based on height,” he said. “If smoke was to rise to the seventh floor, it is not going to stop, and likewise, a fire does not discriminate based on where you are. If someone is disabled on the ground floor, the first floor, the second floor, they are still disabled.
“What are we waiting for, my building, me to burn? What are we waiting for here?”
On a visit to Gabsi’s flat in Harrow, North West London, the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) identified several major concerns, including damp, mould, and – crucial in any evacuation – broken lifts.
Gabsi, who lives on the sixth floor of Trident Point, said he has little confidence that he would make it out alive if there was a fire in the block, which is run by Metropolitan Thames Valley Housing (MTVH).
“If the fire alarm was to ring here, I would have a serious issue with getting outside,” he said. “Previously, I found the evacuation chair to be locked behind a cupboard of which I don’t have the code, which kind of negates the purpose for it.
“I’ve also been told that it can only be used by firefighters, which again doesn’t amount to equal evacuation processes.
“There is a fire safe lift – however, that lift is not working. So what is the point? There is total negligence by by the housing provider and housing association.
“There aren’t arrangements [for a fire]. At this point, I’m going to say a prayer and just stay in my house, to be honest.”
Last month the Fire Committee wrote to the mayor to demand more engagement between social housing landlords and residents.
Chair Anne Clarke, a Labour Assembly member, said: “Nine years after the Grenfell Tower fire, we heard compelling evidence that many social housing residents continue to feel unsafe in their homes. No Londoner should live in fear of fire safety.”
Deputy chair Hina Bokhari, who has long held City Hall to account over the plight of disabled Londoners, said the current situation was “outrageous”.
“What Adam and the residents in this building having to deal with – I’m close to tears,” the Liberal Democrat assembly member told the LDRS.
“If there is a fire here, if something terrible happened here, do we see another Grenfell? Yes – that is my blunt and honest opinion.
“Everybody who lives in high rise flats are at risk. And when it comes to disabled residents, I’m actually really depressed. I feel as if they’re signing a death wish by living here in a high rise flat now.
“Things haven’t moved on since Grenfell – it is absolutely outrageous that we’re in this situation. We still haven’t got accessible housing that is affordable for disabled Londoners. The mayor is not doing his job.”
Gabsi added: “He is pandering to developers rather than really thinking about Londoners – the safety of disabled people should be paramount.
“We not a fringe group, we’re not a small group, and we are the one marginalised group that anyone could join at any time. The fact that this is not being taken seriously is very disappointing.”
What is the mayor doing about it?
City Hall plans to publish a Disability Action Plan next month. The document will make a series of commitments on housing, employment, transport, community safety and accessing services.
A spokesperson for the mayor said: “For many years the mayor strongly lobbied the previous Government to introduce legislation for RPEEPs and welcomed the introduction of this law in April this year.
“He has continued to encourage the government to widen the scope of the new legislation to incorporate all residential blocks and for there to be central funding to pay for them, as well as pushing building owners and landlords to implement these plans as soon as possible.
“It is vital that ministers continue to work with deaf and disabled groups to ensure the legislation and guidance is as effective as it can be, and to monitor how these plans are being implemented across the country. The mayor is also committed to working with the London Fire Brigade and local authorities to ensure disabled Londoners have safe evacuation routes and appropriate support during emergencies.”
An MTVH housing association spokesperson said: “We understand the concerns raised by residents with regards to the issues they have experienced at Trident Point. Their safety and wellbeing is our top priority and we are working closely with them to identify appropriate support to ensure effective arrangements are in place in the event of an emergency evacuation.
“At Trident Point, Personal Emergency Evacuation Plans are in place for residents with identified evacuation needs. We are currently reviewing and updating these plans with residents to ensure they reflect new legal requirements.
“We recognise that there have been intermittent reliability issues with the lifts installed at Trident Point in 2022 and 2023. We continue to work with the lift contractor, landlords and the building’s managing agents, Y&Y and Orbit, to deliver a long-term solution. Whenever a lift outage occurs, we proactively contact affected residents to review support arrangements and determine whether any additional measures are required.
“Leaks, which resulted in water damage, have been resolved. We are now working with Y&Y to complete remedial works and address any remaining damage.”

Although new regulations introduced in April require Residential Personal Emergency Evacuation Plans (RPEEPs), critics argue that height restrictions exclude many vulnerable residents. Issues such as broken lifts, locked evacuation chairs, and housing disrepair have further heightened fears among disabled tenants living in high-rise buildings.
key_points: Fifteen disabled residents died during the 2017 Grenfell Tower fire, prompting inquiry recommendations for personalised evacuation plans.
New RPEEP regulations introduced in April only apply to buildings over 18 metres or specific blocks over 11 metres, excluding tenants in shorter buildings.
Disabled campaigner Adam Gabsi highlighted critical safety issues at Trident Point, including broken lifts and inaccessible evacuation chairs.
The London Assembly Fire Committee and local politicians have criticized current safety measures, warning that disabled high-rise residents remain at severe risk.

title: The new London Plan punishes Barnet
author: Mark Brown
content:
Barnet must not be ‘Boxer’ in Sadiq Khan’s Animal Farm say Cllr Josh Mastin-Lee and Cllr Shimon Ryde
![The outside of the City Hall building in Royal Docks](https://i0.wp.com/barnetpost.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/City-Hall-credit-GLA-1.jpg?resize=812%2C457&ssl=1)
When the Barnet Post published the headline on 17th July “New London Plan includes housing target lower than government’s own aim for the capital” residents breathed a collective sigh of relief.
One can only guess what the headline would have read had the Post’s correspondent known then what we know now, the draft London Plan has burdened Barnet with the highest housing target in the capital, a target even higher than that of the outgoing plan and includes building 7000 homes on Greenbelt land?
Lord Sadiq Khan has released his draft of the new London Plan (effective 2028) which largely determines what gets built and where in London over the next 10 years. If adopted in its current form, his new plan promises to change Barnet beyond recognition.
The highest housing target in London. Our greenbelt given over to developers. A drive towards “site optimisation” which might mean Barnet never builds a house again, only flats. All to bail out London boroughs which have failed to build. Residents and councillors must use the consultation to stand up and make their voices heard.
Barnet’s Conservative Councillors have read and reflected on the draft London Plan. It is deeply troubling. The plan as it is currently authored by the mayor ends Barnet’s long history as a suburban borough. To understand why, here are some of the key reforms in the plan:
- Barnet’s housing target will become the highest in London with a huge rise of 38% against our 2021-2031 target.
- Barnet is expected to build 32,730 “units” in the 10 years between 2028 and 2038.
- Barnet has been told that it should build 7,000 of those units on its greenbelt.
- The plan designates Mill Hill and “Barnet” (meaning Chipping Barnet) as a “Green Belt Broad Location for Growth”, meaning their green spaces could be up for grabs.
- A requirement to “optimise” (i.e. build as many units as possible) small sites with typical heights of 3-4 stories everywhere. It is unlikely that London will ever again build a “house”.
- A new Sustainable Access Measure or “SAM” which replaces Public Transport Accessibility Levels or “PTAL”. PTAL previously helped constrain dense development away from stations.
- The minimum definition of a “tall building” rises from 6 to 10 stories, with a new concept of “Midrise” allowing for higher density.
Together, the above measures would rapidly densify and urbanise Barnet. Consider the huge Edgware development: 28 storey tower blocks and 3,500 flats which will change the town centre forever. Under the new London Plan, Barnet would need to build an “Edgware” every single year.
It means potentially increasing Barnet’s population by almost a quarter (based on average household sizes) in 10 years without any commensurate increase in social or transport infrastructure. In short, Zone 1 density with Zone 6 services.
We can expect developers to pack new schemes with one- and two-bedroom flats rather than the family sized homes needed in Barnet. This is a trend we are increasingly seeing at planning committees with current supply being disproportionately geared towards small flats (“Manhattan apartments” as developers are starting to term them).
Finally, it means releasing hundreds of hectares of our green belt for housing (especially social housing) with yet more to follow in the second 10-year period from 2038 to 2048. This is despite the preservation of our greenbelt being a core tenet of Barnet’s Local Plan.
Looking at the wider London context, we see a great injustice behind Barnet’s targets. Under the current London Plan, Barnet has the fourth highest housing target in London but has also been one of the highest performers in meeting it. This is partly due to extensive regeneration projects in Brent Cross, Colindale and West Hendon, which have used up most of the Borough’s major brownfield sites.
Meanwhile, many other London Boroughs have delivered only a fraction of their housing targets. In the 2021-2024 window, Lewisham delivered only 23% of their target. Greenwich, 39%. Barking & Dagenham, 59%. And yet, the new London Plan has rewarded these boroughs with lower or static housing targets. Lewisham’s target falls by 16%, Greenwich by 1% and Barking & Dagenham by 50%.
What is Barnet’s reward for its own Herculean efforts? It is a significantly higher housing target which consumes our green belt to save the Mayor of London’s blushes. Instead of martialling underperforming London boroughs to do their bit, the mayor has instead dumped the unmet targets on Barnet. No good deed goes unpunished.
There is still time for Barnet’s Councillors and residents to have their say. The draft London Plan is in consultation, ending in mid-October, and we must make our voice heard constructively and persuasively.
As a starting point, we are asking the Mayor of London to extend the consultation (which spans Summer and Jewish High Holy days) to give Barnet a proper chance to review and respond.
At the council level, the Conservatives and Labour are forming a working group alongside planning officers to find common ground for a response. Throughout this process the Conservatives will communicate our concerns repeatedly and robustly.
In parallel, we are working closely with the Conservatives on the London Assembly to deliver a clear message directly to the Mayor of London. That London’s suburbs must be treated as partners in his plan, rather than its workhorse. Barnet must not be ‘Boxer’ in Sadiq Khan’s Animal Farm.
We would also urge Barnet’s residents and residents’ associations to speak out and respond to the consultation. Responses can be sent to [email protected].
In May’s elections, the Conservative and Labour manifestos both promised to protect Barnet’s green belt. Voters entrusted their councillors with a duty of stewardship over Barnet’s precious heritage as a leafy, neighbourly suburb of streets, parks and green fields.
That suburban character is why people come to live in Barnet. They do not come for yet another domineering landscape of standardised, greyish-brown London “block slop”.
By ignoring and even trying to demolish that character, the new London plan might be the greatest test of our stewardship in Barnet’s post-war history. Together, we can and must rise to the challenge as a united front.
