Stay in the loop: sign up for our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox.
summary: The Big Mamma Group is launching its first City of London restaurant, named Edmondo, at 6 Lombard Street in November. Inspired by 1930s Milanese glamour and Villa Necchi Campiglio, the venue features a 200-seat main dining room with an open kitchen and three private dining rooms. The menu will offer Italian fare such as towering focaccia, gnocchi al gorgonzola, spice-crusted steaks, and barrel-aged cocktails.
key_points: Edmondo opens in November at 6 Lombard Street in the City of London.
The restaurant's design is inspired by 1930s Milanese glamour and Villa Necchi Campiglio.
It features a main dining room with an open kitchen and three plush private dining rooms.
Signature menu items include spice-crusted steaks, towering focaccia, and barrel-aged cocktails.

title: Heavy rain hits London as Sadiq Khan warns downpours could lead to 'flash flooding'
author: Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/12/50/IMG_0994.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
According to the national forecaster’s rain tracker, showers began sweeping across the capital from around 12.20pm, and more are expected to come sporadically through this evening.
As much as 32mm of rain per hour fell in parts of the capital, including Hounslow and Woolwich.
The hard, baked ground could make London more susceptible to flash flooding, as Sir Sadiq warned in a post on X.
The mayor wrote: “When heavy rain falls on hard, baked ground, water runs off much more quickly, increasing the risk of flash flooding.”
When severe flash flooding hit London in 2021, rain caused damage and disruption to homes and businesses across the city, with many Londoners forced to stay elsewhere as their homes were flooded with stormwater and sewage.
The mayor also shared government advice, telling Londoners to check the drains outside their homes and to prepare a flood kit.
summary: Heavy rain has hit London, prompting Mayor Sadiq Khan to warn that downpours could lead to flash flooding. Showers began sweeping across the capital around 12.20pm, with rainfall reaching up to 32mm per hour in areas like Hounslow and Woolwich. The mayor noted that hard, baked ground increases the risk of rapid water runoff and urged residents to prepare.
key_points: Heavy rain showers began sweeping across London from around 12.20pm.
Rainfall rates reached up to 32mm per hour in parts of the capital, including Hounslow and Woolwich.
Mayor Sadiq Khan warned that hard, baked ground increases the risk of flash flooding.
Residents were advised to check home drains and prepare a flood kit.

title: The world’s biggest Halal food festival is coming to London next month – with over 200 food vendors from around the world coming to the city
author: Sam Barker
content:
![crowds of people queueing at food stands outside the london stadium, with the iconic ArcelorMittal Orbit slide visible in the background](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/20165640/MJP9607-1024x682.jpg) 
London’s food festival calendar is full to the brim with all manner of exciting foodie experiences. Attendees can explore all manner of different cuisines, dishes, cooking methods, and more. They’re events where visitors can try some of the best food from around the world – all in one place. And next month, the World Halal Food Festival lands in London, celebrating the breadth and diversity of Halal food.
The World Halal Food Festival will take over London Stadium from September 26-27, for a weekend-long celebration of Halal food, culture and commerce.
Based on last year’s success, the World Halal Food Festival 2026 is preparing to welcome more than 200,000 hungry foodies (!). And they’ve got plenty on offer to keep them hungry and sated. The festival will feature over 200 vendors from around the world. There will also be an impressive number of celebrity chefs sharing their knowledge and expertise.
As well as the food, the event will feature “live cooking shows with celebrity chefs, cultural performances, live music, kids’ entertainment, and much more.”
![people watching a cookery demonstration in progress](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/20165650/FOODSEP2024-245-1024x683.jpg)
The World Halal Food Festival 2026
The festival brings together more than 200 food traders from 25 countries around the world. Together they showcase the breadth and possibility of Halal food. There will also be some huge names appearing at the festival, including the likes of:
- Shelina Permaloo (MasterChef: The Professionals winner and culinary ambassador)
- Big Zuu (rapper, presenter, and star of Big Zuu’s Big Eats)
- and a variety of football stars and sporting personalities.
Ensuring that all attendees can enjoy the festival without any concerns, every single vendor and food stall at the World Halal Food Festival is required to serve 100% Halal food. So, you can go along and chow down to your heart’s content!
![presenter, and rapper big zuu talking to people](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/20165655/WHFF-2023_SIMONADSC00241-1024x683.jpg)
What is halal food?
Misinformation has led to some misunderstanding about exactly what is Halal. But it’s actually a fairly simple concept. Almost all food is already Halal, per the International Halal Certification, with the exception of “pork & other Non-Halal animals, carrions, animals slaughtered improperly, ethanol & other intoxicants, and contaminated and hazardous food”.
As processing impacts every aspect of the food we eat, a Halal certification makes it easier for people to know what they can or can’t consume. As the Halal Food Authority explains: “The consumption of halal products is a religious obligation for Muslims, and Halal certification ensures that these products conform to the dietary laws outlined in the Quran and Hadith.”
All sorts of companies and food producers might choose to apply a Halal certification to their products to make people’s decisions easier in shops and restaurants. In doing so, they also join a growing market of consumers. The global halal food and beverage market is valued at $2.24 trillion, and in the UK alone it’s estimated to be worth £40 billion.
![someone biting into some halal food](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/20165645/7SEP2025-240-1024x683.jpg)
🎟️ Grab your ticket to the World Halal Food Festival 2026 here. Entry is free for under-12s. 
📍 London Stadium, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, London, E20 2ST.
🚇 The nearest stations are Hackney Wick, Stratford, and Pudding Mill Lane.
summary: The World Halal Food Festival is coming to London Stadium from September 26-27 for a weekend-long celebration. The event will feature over 200 vendors from 25 countries, celebrity chefs, live cooking shows, cultural performances, and entertainment. Every vendor and food stall at the festival will serve 100% Halal food.
key_points: The festival takes place at London Stadium from September 26-27.
It features over 200 global food vendors and is expected to welcome more than 200,000 visitors.
Every food stall at the event serves 100% Halal food.
Attendees can enjoy live cooking shows with celebrity chefs like Shelina Permaloo and Big Zuu, alongside cultural performances and kids' entertainment.

title: The student survivor who shaped UK's national terrorism memorial day
author: Ewan Somerville
content:
![A man in a black jacket and with glasses, ginger hair and a beard stands on the riverside by the River Thames with Westminster Bridge and the London Eye in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a399/live/36ece130-9c95-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Travis Frain was visiting Westminster as an undergraduate at Edge Hill University when he was caught up in an attack
- Published
Travis Frain was texting his mates a photo he had just taken of Big Ben on a university trip to London when his day turned from normal to anything but.
"One of the guys in my group shouted 'look out' and as I looked up from my phone the terrorist's car was in front of me.
"It was a split second really before the car hit me. I went over the bonnet, into the air, before landing back on the ground."
This was 22 March 2017, when attacker Khalid Masood drove his car into crowds, killing four, before stabbing a police officer to death outside Parliament.
Frain, then 19, was left with multiple injuries including a fractured leg, which took two years to heal. "There will always be a part of you affected by that attack."
Now 28, he spoke to BBC News as the UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism is set to take place on Friday.
'Morally correct to remember'
Mirroring similar fixtures in European countries, the UK government has said the day aims to recognise those impacted by terrorism including victims and their families, witnesses and the emergency services.
At its centre is an event in London on Friday afternoon with a two-minute silence for those lost to terrorism and readings from people affected by it. The event will be staged in locations around the UK in future years.
![Police take security measures at Westminster Bridge after a car ran over people on the bridge during a terror attack. Police tape covers the entrance to the bridge and police vans and officers are seen in the vicinity.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/a117/live/847ff560-9c93-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
The Westminster Bridge attack in 2017 came two months before another major terror attack at an Arianna Grande concert in Manchester arena
Frain, who has campaigned for this day for nearly five years, said he feels recognition and memorials for terror victims "often go under the radar".
"As a society, it is right and morally correct that we should be remembering those lost to terrorism," he said, adding that victims were "often not targeted as individuals but as representatives of something far greater - the nation, the nation's values; the values we're all meant to hold I'm sure."
At the same time, the day will be about encouraging people to "keep an eye on each other" as "we all have a role to play" in stopping terrorism, he added.
In May, the UK's terror threat was raised to "severe", meaning an attack is highly likely. A record nearly 10,000 people were referred to Prevent, the government's anti-terrorism scheme, in the year to September 2025.
![Travis Frain lays on a hospital bed with his leg strapped while King Charles is at his bedside.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/2d5b/live/0c4a8820-9c94-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Travis Frain was visited by Charles, then Prince of Wales, while in hospital
The idea for a national day for terror victims and survivors came about after a Home Office review, external found many needed more support.
But many who have campaigned for the day still feel more needs to be done to help survivors.
A report, released on Friday by the Survivors Against Terror (SAT), said while psychological support for victims had improved, no progress had been made to the state compensation scheme for terror victims, the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority.
SAT's co-founder Brendan Cox, whose wife MP Jo Cox was murdered by a neo-Nazi in 2016, welcomed the national day but warned "survivors also want it to be a moment of accountability".
"We're not talking large sums of money, we're talking about a process that dehumanises people where if you're a survivor of a terror attack, you can only claim for the first three injuries you have despite the fact you have 80 or 90 or 100 pieces of shrapnel in your body," Cox said.
"At the moment we still have members who don't have the resources to build a downstairs toilet following attacks that have left them struggling to walk," added Lisa Ghiggini, who survived the Fishmonger's Hall attack in 2019.
The Ministry of Justice, which is responsible for the taxpayer-funded scheme, where victims self-classify the type of incident, said Â£180m was paid out last year for all types of violent crime including terrorism.
![A young man kneels in front of the floral memorial at Victoria station during the commemoration. Colourful flowers, posters and pictures of Manchester bee icons are shown.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/14d8/live/160a6210-9c97-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Many in Manchester have paid their respects to the victims of the Manchester Arena attack in 2017
The chosen date for the national day of 21 August coincides with the UN International Day of Remembrance and Tribute to the Victims of Terrorism, which began in 2017.
While the UK event will take place in London for its debut year, the Home Office has said people across the country can mark it at home by observing a moment of reflection and sharing posts about the day on social media.
Frain said he knows of many terror survivors who can never return to London, as they remain too harrowed what they experienced in attacks.
He returned to Westminster Bridge just two days after the 2017 attack - while still injured - to "desensitise" himself and he plans to return to the capital on Friday with a similar defiance.
He hopes the King, another royal, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, or a senior cabinet minister will turn up to hear from survivors.
"It's those individuals that provide the national aspect - it can't just be victims in a room talking to one another."
summary: Travis Frain, a survivor of the 2017 Westminster Bridge terror attack, has campaigned for nearly five years to help establish the UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism. Following a Home Office review that highlighted the need for more support, the inaugural event takes place on Friday to recognise those impacted by terrorism, including victims, families, witnesses, and emergency services. While campaigners welcome the national day, they emphasize that more action is needed regarding accountability and improvements to the state compensation scheme.
key_points: Travis Frain was 19 and a university student when he was struck by a car during the 2017 Westminster Bridge attack.
The UK is holding its first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism, coinciding with the UN International Day of Remembrance.
The national day aims to recognize those affected by terrorism, including victims, families, witnesses, and emergency services.
Campaigners and groups like Survivors Against Terror warn that despite better psychological support, the state compensation scheme for terror victims remains flawed and dehumanising.

title: Man of the moment: Nick Jones is back with London’s chicest new hotel
author: Eleanor Steafel
content:
There are a few things you notice immediately. First, the distinct lack of hotel lobby energy. This is no quiet foyer: at 4 pm, it is already humming. Then there are the interiors: cool, contemporary, but somehow cosy, too. It’s like entering a stylish friend’s sitting room on a Friday afternoon, where the only decision you need to make is whether you’d like a cup of tea or a glass of wine. Nick Jones, the founder of Soho House, who redefined luxury by introducing a ‘home away from home’ aesthetic to 1990s London, is attempting to do it again, four years after stepping away from his members’ club empire.
When we meet just a few days into St. Clement’s soft launch, it’s all going rather well. ‘A month ago, it was still a building site,’ says Nick, walking through the busy restaurant, Café Clement. ‘I was hoping it would work when it was full of people – that the acoustics would be right.’ His fears have been allayed. Early reviews have been positive, and the atmosphere is just as he had imagined. ‘People’s reactions are what I’d hoped. I don’t want it to feel like a hotel. The goal is for Café Clement and Bobbi’s bar to be full of people who live and work in the city.’
When Nick left Soho House in 2022 after being diagnosed with prostate cancer (he is now cancer free and a passionate campaigner for a national screening programme), he thought that it was probably time to retire. Then the site on Victoria Embankment came up. Along with his longtime collaborator Mark Wadhwa, he went back into the fray. ‘I figured we could try to reinvent what a modern-day luxury hotel could be.’
A laid-back luxe vibe has been Nick’s calling card for decades, so it makes sense that St. Clement feels so comfortable. Decorated by Eagle + Hodges, the firm helmed by Mark’s wife, Alex Eagle, and Sophie Hodges, guest rooms are dressed in calming palettes and have well-appointed bathrooms with chic, full-size products that guests are welcome to take away with them. Capping the newbuild hotel is an extraordinary penthouse and 14 apartment-like River Lofts, with views from Canary Wharf in the east to Battersea Power Station in the west.
It’s impressive but, as Nick acknowledges, there’s been ‘an avalanche of upscale brands coming to London’ and he wants St. Clement to be an institution. That means getting the restaurant and the bar right. ‘Café Clement is like a version of the first restaurant that ever worked for me in London – Café Bohème,’ he says. Open from 7 am until late (as Café Clement will be), it offered a quick coffee, a solo omelette, or a multi-course feast. ‘We want people to use Café Clement two or three times a week – for lunch, breakfast, drinks or hanging out in the garden.’
The menu – by chef Danny Bohan, whom Nick brought over from his favourite restaurant, The River Café – begins with everything you could want at breakfast and leads into fresh takes on classics: steak with anchovy hollandaise, Parmesan custard with caviar, roasted fish, tempting pastas.
Across the lobby, Bobbi’s is far cooler than the usual hotel bar, with a Devon Turnbull sound system and shelves filled with vinyl. ‘Alex and Sophie really pushed me,’ says Nick. ‘If I went into Soho House territory with a fabric or paint colour, they would say, “We don’t want to do that – this is a new thing, a new chapter.”’
They have succeeded. The hotel has an unmistakable Nick Jones feel about it, but this is no Soho House mark two. Nor is it destined to become a new empire for him. ‘I want to have a smaller life and do less,’ he says. As I leave him in the bar, where people stop to shake his hand and congratulate him on St. Clement, a quiet life doesn’t seem all that likely.
Rooms at St. Clement cost from £600: stclement.co.uk
summary: Nick Jones, the founder of Soho House, has returned to London's hospitality scene with the launch of his new hotel, St. Clement. Located on Victoria Embankment, the property features a laid-back, contemporary aesthetic designed to feel like a home rather than a traditional hotel. Jones partnered with longtime collaborator Mark Wadhwa and designers Alex Eagle and Sophie Hodges to create the new space, which includes the restaurant Café Clement and the bar Bobbi's.
key_points: Nick Jones has opened a new London hotel called St. Clement, four years after stepping away from Soho House.
The hotel's design aims to avoid traditional lobby energy, offering a cozy, contemporary aesthetic created by designers Alex Eagle and Sophie Hodges.
St. Clement features Café Clement, led by chef Danny Bohan, and Bobbi's bar, which includes a Devon Turnbull sound system and vinyl collection.
Rooms at the new hotel start at £600 per night.

title: Green light for US billionaire’s London science institute HQ plan
author: Rockwool
content:
Westminster signs off Foster’s refurb of listed townhouse site on St James’s Square for Larry Ellison
Westminster council has unanimously approved Foster + Partners’ designs for a refurbishment of a listed townhouse site on St James’s Square as the head office of a science institue set up by the world’s sixth richest man.
The Ellison Institute of Technology (EIT) is an advanced research body set up by Larry Ellison, the former chief executive of software company Oracle Corporation.
EIT, which describes itself as multi-disciplinary science institute, is currently building a £300m science research facility in Oxford that has been designed by Fosters with the first phase being built by Laing O’Rourke.
The organisation’s London headquarters will transform two grade II and grade II*-listed buildings at 11-12 St James’s Square and rebuild an extension to the rear of the site that was completed in 1990.
The scheme would retrofit the existing historic buildings and knock down the rear extension, adding new lifts, showers, cycle storage space, new glazed facades and terraces and reinstating a historic garden at ground level.
The job is due to be carried out by Sir Robert McAlpine after the firm beat Multiplex to the work earlier this year. Described as “very high spec”, it is understood to have a price tag of around £120m. Others to look at the job were Mace and McLaren.
Other firms working on the plan, which was sent in to Westminster city council in January, include development manager Edit, planning consultant Avison Young, heritage consultant Donald Insall Associates and project manager Ridge.
According to Bloomberg, Ellison is worth $198bn (£145bn) and remains the largest shareholder of Oracle.
summary: Westminster Council has unanimously approved Foster + Partners' design to refurbish listed townhouses on St James's Square into the London headquarters for the Ellison Institute of Technology. The approximately £120m project, to be carried out by Sir Robert McAlpine, involves retrofitting historic buildings and rebuilding a rear extension. The institute is an advanced research body established by billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison.
key_points: Westminster Council unanimously approved Foster + Partners' plans for the EIT London headquarters.
The project involves refurbishing listed buildings at 11-12 St James's Square and rebuilding a 1990s rear extension.
Sir Robert McAlpine is slated to carry out the approximately £120m high-specification construction job.
The Ellison Institute of Technology is an advanced research body founded by billionaire Larry Ellison.

title: Most Londoners don't want Sadiq Khan to contest fourth mayoral election - poll
author: Rachael Burford; Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Sadiq Khan reflects on ULEZ, Trump feud, running for London Mayor again, and wanting to manage Liverpool](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/07/16/16/f3930ae22a488e1ef94b16fad2b22e35Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg0MzAwOTk3-2.84969890.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
In a blow to Sir Sadiq, the YouGov survey released on Thursday found 56% of people living in the capital think he should step down and allow a different Labour candidate to contest the next mayoral election, due in May 2028.
This includes almost a third (31%) of those who supported him at the last vote in 2024.
More than half of Londoners 55% say they believe the city has become a worse place to live since Sir Sadiq was first elected 10 year ago.
![Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan said the research ‘proves we were right to act’ (Victoria Jones/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/07/6cf18c2a55353082ea87aedde5a23035Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MTQ0ODM2-2.75224103.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Only 5% of people surveyed thought the amount of affordable housing in London had improved over the last decade.
This is compared to three quarters (76%) who said it had got worse, despite Sir Sadiq vowing that building more homes would be his “single biggest priority” when he first entered City Hall in 2016.
Londoners were also more likely to report conditions declining when it came to the economy and jobs (69%), homelessness (62%), high streets and public spaces (62%) and crime (58%).
Sir Sadiq is yet to confirm whether he will stand for a fourth term after winning a landslide victory in 2024.
But there are understood to be several high profile Labour politicians who want to take on the job, including former foreign secretary David Lammy and Brent East MP Dawn Butler.
A recent poll for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London (QMUL), found Sir Sadiq would win a fourth term if he stood despite a surge in support for the Greens, according to a new poll.
Read More
The latest YouGov survey was not all bad news for the incumbent Mayor.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/13/29/image004.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Some 37% of people said they believed public transport had got better in the city over the last ten year, compared to 27% who think it has stayed the same and 30% who said it had gotten worse.
Overall, 40% of Londoners think Sir Sadiq has done a good job over the decade, compared to 47% who say he has done a bad job.
The poll also showed 42% of people believe he has done a better job as Mayor than his predecessor Boris Johnson.
Less than a third of people (31%) said he has done a worse job than Mr Johnson.
Matthew Smith, YouGov data journalist, said: “While Sadiq Khan has a reasonably high favourability rating among Londoners, at least for a politician, only 24% of them think he should run for a fourth term as Mayor of London.
“This compares to the 56% who think he should let a different Labour candidate contest that election, which is scheduled for May 2028.
“Among those who voted Labour at the last general election 39% think he should run again, compared to 41% who think he should stand down.”
The Mayor of London’s office was contacted for comment.
summary: A YouGov survey indicates that 56% of Londoners believe Mayor Sadiq Khan should step down and allow another Labour candidate to run in the May 2028 election. Over half of residents surveyed feel the city has worsened since he took office a decade ago, citing declines in affordable housing, the economy, and crime. However, positive findings include 37% who believe public transport has improved and 42% who rate his performance better than his predecessor, Boris Johnson.
key_points: 56% of Londoners surveyed think Sadiq Khan should step down instead of contesting a fourth mayoral term in 2028.
55% of residents believe London has become a worse place to live since he was first elected 10 years ago.
76% of respondents reported that affordable housing has worsened over the last decade.
37% of people believe public transport has improved under his tenure.
42% of Londoners feel he has done a better job as mayor than Boris Johnson, compared to 31% who think he has done worse.

title: London Playbook PM: Manual shrift
author: Emilio Casalicchio
content:
Good afternoon. This is Emilio Casalicchio.
THURSDAY CHEAT SHEET
— Andy Burnham defended the controversial Home Office guide telling asylum seekers that rape is illegal.
— The PM vowed to make illegal waste-dumpers clean up their mess.
— The Lib Dems are peeved and Reform is pleased that Burnham has bottled a political donations cap.
— Lucy Powell insisted her plans to save kids from multiple GCSE resits are not dumbing down education.
— Burnham said protection for Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will be “a private matter” when the pair return to Britain.
TOP OF THE NEWSLIST
MANUAL SHRIFT: Andy Burnham defended the under-fire Home Office manual telling asylum seekers that rape and pedophilia are illegal in Britain.
No excuses: The PM suggested, during a visit to an illegal waste dump in Bradford, that the controversial leaflet will leave foreign national offenders earmarked for deportation with no excuse. “I’m currently working to ensure that foreign national offenders who can be removed from the prison system are removed from that system,” he told a TV clip this afternoon. “So it follows that if we’re taking this approach, it’s made explicitly clear what the U.K. law is and what the societal norms of the U.K. are, and that’s why this approach is being taken.”
Nevertheless: Criticism that the nine-page instruction booklet is even required continues to wash in from the right. “Anyone needing this leaflet does not belong in Britain,” Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said on social media. “I’ve been warning for a long time that not all cultures are equal. Britain can be proudly multi-ethnic, but we should not be multi-cultural.”
It goes without writing in a niche political newsletter: Reform’s home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf responded to Conservative outrage with a list of illegal migrant rapists and murderers who entered Britain while the Tories were in power. Nice, light debate to be having over summer, this.
Worth bearing in mind: There is zero evidence that migration levels impact violent crime rates, according to the Oxford Uni Migration Observatory. This episode of More or Less from three months ago also tackled the issue, prompted by a false claim from commentator Annunziata Rees-Mogg that asylum seekers committed 44 percent of alleged sex offenses in Dorset. She’d asked AI to check the claim, which, of course, told her it was correct. 🤦
And lo: The hard left is attacking the Home Office for singling out asylum seekers in the booklet. “This is a dangerous and unnecessary move by the Home Office which feeds into right-wing tropes, and fuels the misinformation around migrants and people seeking asylum which has resulted in violent protests outside places where migrants are being housed, and attacks on migrants themselves,” said Green Peer Jenny Jones.
So it’s also worth pointing out: Former Safeguarding and Violence Against Women and Girls Minister Jess Phillips told Times Radio the government also runs “multi-million-pound” campaigns to remind British men about sexual consent, harassment and stalking, while U.K. schools teach kids about healthy relationships. Equalites Secretary Bridget Phillipson meanwhile told the Guardian social media is normalizing sexism (and racism) in Britain.
The Home Office line: Officials insist those who break the law face removal — and point to the latest deportation stats out overnight. “We expect everyone who comes to the U.K. to abide by our laws,” a spokesperson said. “If they do not, they will face consequences, including the refusal of their asylum claim and removal from the U.K. Returns of failed asylum seekers have reached their highest level since 2010 under this government.”
DRIVETIME DEBRIEF
REFUSE TO BUDGE: Andy Burnham vowed to put fly-tippers to work in community clean-up squads and allow councils to chase offenders for waste-clearance bills — plans the government launched an eight-week consultation on this afternoon. (So much for ending consultation culture.) The idea is to deliver justice while avoiding protracted court proceedings. Here’s the obligatory Burnham social media clip from his visit to Bradford.
CAP TIN-EARED: Our scoop that Burnham won’t impose a cap on political donations has bombed among those hoping to clean up politics. The Lib Dems said British democracy is being left “dangerously exposed” and urged frustrated Labour MPs to back their amendment creating a commission to investigate the merits of a cap. The Burnham stance is, however, going down better with unions, which would see potential donations to Labour drastically curtailed under the proposals from *checks notes* Labour MPs.
Cap in hand: One union leader insisted British unions funding our politics is different to, say, a crypto-billionaire based in Thailand throwing cash at U.K. parties. “It is fundamentally different, somebody handing over a cheque for £5 million, and a supermarket worker volunteering to pay 50p a week towards politics,” the person said — noting that decisions on union donations are collectively taken and publicly declared. “Our policy agenda is not hidden away,” the person added. “We have bloody conferences every year where we say upfront to politicians, this is what we want to see.”
Also pleased: A Reform official said Burnham bottling a donations cap is “very good news for us.”
Now watch this: The Democracy for Sale Substack has launched a video series about political mega-donors.
THE ANTI-UNI-PARTY: Reform education spokesperson Suella Braverman told kids receiving their GCSE results this morning to avoid being “ripped off by the great university scam. Don’t waste your time studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university. If you want to work hard, if you want to move forward, earn a wage, and have opportunities in your life, take up and look for apprentices.” She made the comments at a press conference in Enfield.
As such … a Reform government would stump up 30 percent of apprentice wages for small and medium-sized businesses, in a bid to recruit an annual 600,000 new apprentices before 2034 — paid for via borrowing. Workers who remain at a firm for two years after completing an apprenticeship would also get a £2,000 bonus. It’s all in this Reform proposal document, which includes a pledge to ban government loans for foreign students.
Grade out: Elsewhere in the GCSEs fallout, former Education Sec Michael Gove accused the government of lowering educational standards, after successor Lucy Powell vowed to create alternatives to English and Maths resits. He told Times Radio a “culture of low expectations … lets children down,” adding: “It is a moral imperative for this country to demand that we end illiteracy and innumeracy, and it is absolutely vital that the education secretary should be leading a crusade to get more children to pass examinations. There is nothing physiological or neurological or in social circumstances that prevents you getting a pass in GCSE English or maths.”
But but but: Powell told Radio 4 this morning the resit treadmill is “throwing tens of thousands of young people on the scrap heap” who could pursue other routes to good careers. She insisted her plan, for “stepping-stone” qualifications, allowing kids who fail their GCSEs to show numeracy and literacy skills to employers and colleges, is not about lowering standards.
On which note: The GCSE pass rate fell a little for the fifth year in a row, but more kids achieved the highest grades across England, Wales and Northern Ireland. The Beeb has more.
REPORTS OUT THIS AFTERNOON: Think Labour (which used to be Labour Together) has a paper out about laws gumming up the state and making issues like the prisons crisis harder to solve. It comes as new stats this week suggested there are fewer than 1,800 prison places available in England and Wales — the lowest level since March. The BBC has a writeup.
OH, AND … Andy Burnham told his TV clip in Bradford that security for Prince Harry and Meghan Markle on their return to the U.K. is a “private matter” and “we wish them well.” Our Isabel Loubser has listed the five awkward questions as the pair plot their homecoming. And tax expert Dan Neidle flagged a wonderful tax angle.
**The future of energy will be shaped by today's decisions. Discover the ONS 2026 programme, where world leaders, ministers, CEOs and experts meet to discuss energy security, climate, technology and geopolitics. Learn more.**
SOCIAL (MEDIA) AFFAIRS
WELL WORTH A READ: The BBC’s Matt Chorley has a great feature about politicians in the social media age, as we acclimatize to the most online PM we’ve ever had.
THE LIVE-ACTION REFORM MELTDOWN CONTINUES: Zia Yusuf posted a 278-word tweet about why claims about his popularity are apparently wrong. He labelled the post “important.” Tim Shipman was quick to hit back on the same site, with his big piece about Reform infighting landing in the Spectator overnight. The biggest beneficiary of these fun-but-pointless squabbles on X is, of course, Elon Musk.
DOES THIS COUNT AS ONE OF THE NINE LIVES? Photographer (and political commentator) Steve Back said his Twitter account got hacked, after his account last night posted (now deleted) that Larry the cat had died.
BEYOND THE M25
HITTING BACK: Israel’s Foreign Affairs minister accused Ed Miliband of using a “patronising tone” when he wrote that putting E1 settlement project construction contracts out to tender was “unacceptable and destructive”. The plans, international humanitarian organizations say, are illegal under international law and violate article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention. But Gideon Sa’ar said Miliband’s statement is “entirely one-sided”, adding that it was “absurd for Britain to lecture the Jewish people”, when the country still controls distant colonial territories.
WE’LL TAKE THE UPGRADE: First minister John Swinney has spent the day trying to explain why he spent £45,000 in taxpayer money on flights to the World Cup in Boston for him and two senior aides. He did some work post-game, attending trade talks in Kentucky, and Justice Secretary Neil Gray said the upgraded flights make sure ministers “arrive fresh”. Sports Minister Maree Todd was amongst another contingent clearly judged not to need this “freshness” — they flew economy. More from the BBC here.
UNDER INVESTIGATION: Nathan Cofnas, the academic who raised concerns over Jason Arday’s work and qualifications, has been suspended from Ghent University. Cofnas has previously been the subject of controversy. In 2024, he published a Substack article claiming that intelligence and race are linked and that black academics were only given jobs at Harvard due to DEI programmes. The University of Cambridge later fired him.
COURT CIRCULAR: A man named Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim was charged in connection with the Heaton Park synagogue attack in Manchester last October.
TONIGHT’S MEDIA ROUND
LEADING THE NEWS BULLETINS: Channel 5 News (5 p.m.) reports on reverse Megxit.
BBC PM (Radio 4, 5 p.m.): Barrister Cherie Blair.
GB News Tonight (GB News, 7 p.m.): Reform UK Home Affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf.
Jacob Rees-Mogg’s State of the Nation (GB News, 8 p.m.): Labour MP Karl Turner.
Patrick Christys Tonight (GB News, 9 p.m.): Tory peer Shaun Bailey.
REVIEWING THE PAPERS TONIGHT: Sky News (10 p.m.): The New Statesman’s Rachel Cunliffe and More in Common Director Luke Tryl … Times Radio (10.30 p.m.): Former Tory MP Julie Kirkbride and PoliticsHome’s Adam Payne.
TOMORROW’S WORLD
DEBT ON ARRIVAL: The latest debt and borrowing stats drop from the Office for National Statistics at 7 a.m.
WHAT THE GOVERNMENT WANTS TO TALK ABOUT: Victims and survivors of terrorism.
WHAT THE CONSERVATIVES WANT TO TALK ABOUT: Kemi Badenoch is expected to appear in Scotland to chat farming.
ANY OTHER BUSINESS
SPOTTED: Influencer Molly-Mae Hague filming near the Westminster Arms pub, as civil servants watched on.
NEW GIG: Reform MP Robert Jenrick has hired Mitchell Palmer from the Adam Smith Institute to be his economics adviser, the Speccie’s James Heale revealed this morning.
WHAT I’VE BEEN READING: The London Centric piece about how landlords and estate agents are getting around a ban on rental bidding wars in the Renters’ Rights Act. Now homes are being advertised at inflated prices in the hope panicked would-be tenants stump up over the odds, or out-bid each other below the astronomical asking prices.
PACKED LUNCH OR PALACE LUNCH: It’s recess! Make the most of a quieter Westminster with a stroll around to check out the menus.
ON THIS DAY IN POLITICS: On Aug. 20, 1945 future Labour leader (and election loser) Michael Foot made his maiden speech in the Commons. More here from the Tides of History account on Instagram.
WRITING PLAYBOOK TOMORROW MORNING: Sam Francis.

summary: Andy Burnham defended a controversial Home Office guide informing asylum seekers that rape and pedophilia are illegal, while pushing plans to make illegal waste-dumpers clean up community sites. The government launched a consultation on the fly-tipping proposals and faced criticism for declining to impose a cap on political donations. Meanwhile, political reactions followed Reform's education proposals and debate over GCSE resit alternatives.
key_points: Andy Burnham defended a Home Office manual clarifying that rape and pedophilia are illegal for asylum seekers.
The government launched an eight-week consultation on plans to force illegal waste-dumpers into community clean-up squads.
Burnham decided against imposing a cap on political donations, drawing criticism from the Lib Dems but approval from unions.
Reform proposed funding 30 percent of apprentice wages for small and medium-sized businesses through borrowing.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell defended plans for alternative stepping-stone qualifications instead of mandatory GCSE resits.

Some 43.4% of exam entries within Richmond upon Thames were awarded grade 7 or above, up from 43.2% in 2025, according to data published by Ofqual. It was the second best performing local authority in the country.
It was followed by Sutton (43.0%) and Kingston upon Thames (42.5%) in third and fourth places nationally.
Barnet made it into the top 10 with 37.4% of entries getting grade 7 or above.
Scroll down for a full list of the ranking of London boroughs, and a separate list of how they rank nationally.
The top performing local authority in the country was Cambridge with 53.5% of exam entries getting top grades, up from 50.3% in 2025.
The local area in England with the lowest proportion of GCSE entries getting an 7 or above this year is Tamworth in Staffordshire, on 6.7%, followed by Knowsley in Merseyside (8.3%), Burnley in Lancashire (9.2%), Havant in Hampshire (9.5%) and Pendle in Lancashire (9.5%).
Within London the lowest ranked were Barking & Dagenham (20.4%) and Havering (19.0%).

title: I went to London’s brand new Peaky Blinders experience – this is what it’s like
author: Andrzej Lukowski
content:
[title]
It’s a testament to the endless iconographic appeal of Steven Knight’s Brummie gangland drama that Peaky Blinders: Underworld isn’t even the first immersive Peaky Blinders experience to run in London – that honour went to Peaky Blinders: The Rise, a show so awful I prayed the Shelby gang would drag me out of it and shoot me dead.
Peaky Blinders: Underworld is a very different, greatly improved kettle of fish which doesn’t even use the word ‘immersive’ in its marketing, although to all intents and purposes that’s what it is. (To be clear, it’s made by completely different people, being attributed to the rather inscrutable ‘KMJ Entertainment in partnership with Banijay Rights’).
Made with the blessing of show creator Steven Knight what’s unusual is the fact that Underworld is divided into two sections, one of which is free. Or free-ish: it’s a pub. You don’t have to pay entry to be admitted to The Garrison, which is nominally a recreation of the Victorian boozer that serves as the Shelby gang’s HQ in the show. But to be clear, the pints are very definitely not 1920s prices (that would be about 2p a go).
![Peaky Blinders: Underworld, 2026](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438490/image.webp) 
Built into the London Bridge arches in what I believe is the old location of Southwark Playhouse, I found The Garrison a slightly weird concept: you can’t faithfully magic up an historic pub just like that. It is ultimately a Peaky Blinders theme pub. Still, I wouldn’t rule out a casual pint here if I was in the area: it’s spacious, the period details are clearly faux but for the most part atmospheric rather than tacky (wooden boards, wooden bar, proper barstool, costumed barstaff), and it happily continues the show’s anachronistic music policy with Nick Cave et al on the jukebox and live bands playing several nights a week. There’s also the odd actor barking at us in an enjoyably flinty Brummie accent, although you won’t really get any story in this bit.
The question, then, is whether or not to step into the Underworld, which is the immersive experience behind the pub. Presumably most punters will in fact have prepaid, but I’d assume it’s possible that after a few pints a casual Garrison punter might find themselves spontaneously signing up for the experience.
The pints are very definitely not 1920s prices
Behind the doors, then, is a polished immersive walkthrough area that boils the Birmingham of the show down to its lurid highlights: the fairground; Chinatown; the bookies; the tattoo parlour that is also a bar – that sort of thing. I was given what I’m going to call an activity book upon entry, which has little tokens that enable you to claim a go on each of the fairground games (hook a duck, that sort of thing), plus you can also take on one (or I think more) of several bigger challenges, though on the opening night the only one available was ‘Catch the Rat’, which as you can probably imagine had little to do with rodent control. Although the task was given to me by another appreciably hard-nosed, hard-accented Blinders gang member, the actual job required following clues and solving puzzles in a way that presumably has little bearing on how one actually catches a rat. No rats were harmed in the making of this show. It’s gentle puzzle solving, basically, though the good news is I won a drinks voucher for completing it (I’m not clear if every winner does so).
![Peaky Blinders: Underworld, 2026](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438497/image.webp) 
I think the key things to bear in mind here are that one, the Underworld isn’t particularly massive – you can’t lose yourself in it like a Punchdrunk show – and two, you’re not really getting a great story, just a fairly standard immersive theatre/escape room-style puzzle chain. But it goes about it in a very fun, very atmospheric, very nicely designed way, and if you love that Blinders iconography via the medium of a well-crafted immersive set with some modest lateral thinking thrown in, then it should do it for you. Tickets are around £25 for a one-hour timeslot - some might consider that a bit steep for pottering around a few rooms, but if you get into the quest and are game for the games you’ll have a diverting time (and the prospect of winning a drink takes the edge off the price a bit).
The dirty secret is that obviously nobody – well, almost nobody – really wants to go back to 1920s Birmingham to work for a criminal gang and that is not what Underworld is offering. It’s an opportunity to sink a few tankards, play a few games and be barked at by some impassive Brummie gangsters. If that’s your idea of a good day out then you’ve just found your new favourite London destination.
Peaky Blinders: Underworld is at the London Bridge Arches, just off Tooley St.

summary: Peaky Blinders: Underworld is a new immersive experience located in the London Bridge arches, created with the blessing of show creator Steven Knight. It is divided into two sections: a free-to-enter themed pub called The Garrison and a ticketed, one-hour immersive walkthrough area featuring sets, games, and puzzles. While it does not offer a deep narrative, the experience delivers a fun, atmospheric, and nicely designed outing for fans of the show's iconography.
key_points: The experience is located in the London Bridge arches in the former Southwark Playhouse space.
The Garrison is a spacious, themed Victorian-style pub with free entry and live music, though drinks are modern-priced.
The ticketed Underworld section costs around £25 for a one-hour timeslot and features fairground games, themed rooms, and gentle puzzle solving.
Participants can win drinks vouchers by completing challenges like the 'Catch the Rat' puzzle.
The attraction is produced by KMJ Entertainment in partnership with Banijay Rights with Steven Knight's blessing.
